target_only_tests.note: Fifteen cases, none counted as ported coverage, in three groups. Every one was measured red under a named mutation and green again on revert (docs/test-translation-conventions.md rule 10), and each measurement is quoted with its probe id below; the two entries above carry P1 and P2. GROUP 1 -- the rest of the fail-closed repair (four cases, D-0904). The source has FOUR silent recovery paths and interlock's own suite pins only two of them, so inverting only the two ported cases would leave half the repaired defect unprotected. `a blank file is refused` (P3: replacing the refusal with `return new DedupState()` turns it red, `expected DedupStateRefused to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`) -- the source returns empty state for a whitespace-only file without even a warning, and since `saveState` writes through a fully-written temporary and a rename it never produces one, so a blank file at that path is a truncation from outside. `an unreadable file is refused` (P4, same measured message) -- the source's `except OSError` branch; the case puts a DIRECTORY where the state file belongs so `readFileSync` raises `EISDIR`, chosen over a `chmod 000` file because a suite that happens to run as root reads a 0000 file happily and the case would pass for the wrong reason. `a namespace that is present but not an object is refused` (P5: substituting `emptyNamespace()` turns it red) -- the source's `data.get("events") if isinstance(..., dict) else {}` is the repaired defect at a narrower scope, and the case runs three shapes (`42`, `["a"]`, `null`). `a namespace entry that is not a string is refused` (P6: `String(entry)` plus a `continue` turns it red) -- the source's `{k: str(v) ... if v is not None}` both coerces a number into a timestamp string and silently DROPS a null entry, and a dropped entry is one already-notified key forgotten; three shapes again (a number, a null, an object). GROUP 2 -- rule 9, the port's types being wider than the source's (five cases). `a dedup key naming an Object.prototype member is not already notified` and `a key naming an Object.prototype member round-trips through the file`: the dedup key is caller-supplied (an `events.id`, a `task_id`) and Python's `dict` has no inherited keys, so `state.events["constructor"]` on an object literal is truthy for a state nobody has written and the event is suppressed FOREVER. Measured precisely, because the two defences are independent and the honest statement is not the flattering one: under `Object.create(null)` alone or `Object.hasOwn` alone each remaining defence still answers correctly, so P7 (namespaces built as `{}`) turns only the round-trip case red, P7b (`Object.hasOwn` replaced by an `=== undefined` check) turns NEITHER red, and the combined mutation turns both red. Both defences are kept and both cases are kept; the round-trip case is the one that fails on the single most likely regression, which is a rebuild site constructing a plain object. `a cooldown that is not a non-negative integer is refused` (P8: removing the guard turns it red): `cooldown_sec` is `int` in the source, so CPython excludes `NaN` and the infinities by construction, and a `NaN` cooldown makes every `>=` comparison false -- pending notifications silently suppressed for the life of the process with nothing red anywhere. `a recorded timestamp is spelled the way datetime.isoformat spells it` (P9: returning `Date#toISOString` turns it red, `expected '2026-05-12T12:00:00.000Z' to be '2026-05-12T12:00:00Z'`): `datetime.isoformat` prints no fractional part at zero microseconds and six digits otherwise, `toISOString` always prints three, and the stored text is a durable value another reader parses. `an instant datetime could not hold is refused rather than recorded` (P10: removing the guard turns it red): `new Date(NaN)` and a year past 9999 are values this runtime admits and `datetime` excludes, and either written into the file is a key whose cooldown can never be evaluated again. GROUP 3 -- properties the source has and its own suite does not reach (six cases). `a stored timestamp is read by fromisoformat's grammar, not Date.parse's` and `a naive stored timestamp is read as UTC, not as the runner's local time` (P11: replacing `parseIso` with `new Date(text)` turns BOTH red, the first `expected false to be true` and the second `expected true to be false`): the source's one garbled literal is refused by both readers, so `test_pending_garbled_timestamp_allows_notify` cannot tell the two apart; `"05/12/2026 11:59:00"` and `"2026-02-30T11:59:00Z"` are accepted or rolled forward by `Date.parse` and raise in `fromisoformat`, and a naive value is LOCAL time here and UTC there -- every one of them turns a garbled stored value into a recent one and BLOCKS the notification the ported case exists to let through, and the naive one does it by the runner's timezone offset, which is a green suite in one region and a red one in another. `a failed write leaves no temporary file behind` (P12: removing the `unlinkSync` turns it red, `expected [ Array(1) ] to deeply equal []`): the source's `except OSError: unlink(tmp); raise`, which its own atomic-save case never exercises. This case is also rule 10's own worked example in miniature: the FIRST draft made the serialiser throw, which happens before the temporary file is created, and the probe measured it GREEN with the unlink removed -- a case that could never have failed. It was rewritten to fail the RENAME instead (a non-empty directory standing where the state file belongs), which is the one step that runs with the temporary already on disk, and only then did P12 turn it red. THE LAST THREE WERE ADDED BY THE CODEX REVIEW GATE'S FIRST ROUND, each closing a defect the twelve above did not reach, and each with its own probe. `a byte that is not UTF-8 is refused even inside a valid JSON string` (probe R1: restoring `readFileSync(path, "utf8")` turns it red, `expected DedupStateRefused to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`). This one contradicted a claim an earlier draft of this ledger made, and the correction is the point: the draft said an undecodable file reaches a refusal either way, at the JSON parse. It does not. A bad byte INSIDE a JSON string leaves the document syntactically valid, `readFileSync`'s utf8 mode substitutes U+FFFD, the parse succeeds, and the state loads carrying a dedup key that is not the key that was written -- an already-notified event free to fire again, which is the exact outcome D-0904's repair exists to prevent, arriving through the repair's own reader. The file is now read as bytes and decoded with a fatal `TextDecoder`. `an invalid now is refused rather than suppressing the notification` (probe R2: removing the guard turns it red) is rule 9 on the CLOCK argument rather than on the cooldown: `new Date(NaN).getTime()` is `NaN`, so the comparison is false for every key at every age, and `recordNotified` already refused the same value through `pyIsoUtc` while the read path did not. `the stored-timestamp grammar is fromisoformat's, measured against CPython` (probes R3 and R3b: removing the week-date branch turns it red on `2026-W20-2`, removing the basic-format time branch on `20260512T115900`) is the largest of the three. `datetime.fromisoformat` on CPython 3.12 accepts far more than the shape a translation reaches for first: basic format (`20260512`, `115900`), ISO week dates (`2026-W20-2`, `2026W202`, `2026-W20`), an hour-only or hour-and-minute time, ANY single character as the date/time separator, a two-digit-hour offset, a sub-second offset, and a fractional second truncated rather than rounded at six digits. Every form the first transcription left out is a stored value this port would have read as garbled while the source read it as a real timestamp -- an extra notification where the source applies the cooldown. The grammar was re-derived by MEASUREMENT, not by recall: 68 inputs were run through `datetime.fromisoformat` on CPython 3.12.3 (the interpreter interlock's suite runs on at 65f36c5) and against this port's `parseIso`, and all 68 now agree; 26 of them are pinned in the case, chosen as the rows that separate this grammar from the naive one plus the refusals that must stay refusals. THE GRAMMAR CASE GREW AGAIN IN THE GATE'S SECOND ROUND, which found four more divergences the first round's 68-input differential had not covered, each measured against CPython 3.12.3 and each pinned by a row and a probe. (1) An ISO week can resolve OUTSIDE `datetime`'s own year range: `9999-W52-7` is `year 10000 is out of range` there, and this port produced `+010000-01-02T00:00:00.000Z` (probe S1). That one is the dangerous direction -- a garbled stored value read as a FUTURE instant, which SUPPRESSES the notification rather than taking the garbled path that lets it through. (2) `Date.UTC(1, 0, 4)` is 1901, so a week date in the first century resolved against the wrong January: `0001-W01-1` came back as `1900-12-31` (probe S2). `parseIso` already undid that remapping for calendar dates; the week resolver did not, which is rule 11's own shape -- a repair applied at one entry point and not at the sibling. (3) A UTC offset whose hour, minute and second components are ALL zero discards its fraction in CPython, so `+00:00:00.5` is plain UTC while `+00:00:02.25` is 2.25 seconds; without the quirk the instant moved 500ms (probe S3), three orders of magnitude past the sub-millisecond rounding this ledger discloses. (4) The date/time separator is ONE character to Python, which indexes a `str` by code point, and two UTF-16 units here when it is astral: `slice(1)` left half a surrogate pair in front of the time and turned a timestamp CPython reads into a garbled one (probe S4). The differential set was extended to 90 inputs and all 90 now agree; the case's table carries eight of the new rows.

notes: `approved_non_running` is empty because the file uses no non-running construct. Checked directly against scripts/parity-check.mjs's own NON_RUNNING patterns -- `(test|it|describe).skip`, `(test|it|describe).todo`, `(test|it).fails`, `skipIf(` and `xfail(` -- over test/attention/dedup.test.ts with comments and string literals INCLUDED, which is stricter than the sweep: no match. The source has no capability gate to carry and the port adds none; every case here runs on every platform the suite runs on. `conditionally_collected` is empty for the same reason: nothing here is absent from a host's collection, and all 10 mapped ids plus the 12 target-only ones were present in `vitest list --json` when this ledger was written (22 collected from this file, 22 passed).

THE RULE 9 ANSWERS, which `docs/test-translation-conventions.md` requires in the porting report. (1) WHICH CALLER-SUPPLIED STRINGS ARE USED AS A MAP KEY: the dedup key, in both namespaces, on all four paths -- `shouldNotify`'s lookup, `recordNotified`'s write, the JSON reader's copy and `saveState`'s dump. It reaches the module unfiltered (`event:<events.id>` and `pending:<task_id>:<kind>`), so both namespaces are built with `Object.create(null)` and read with `Object.hasOwn`, and two target-only cases pin it. The document's own two field names (`events`, `pending`) are read with `getOwn` for the same reason, though neither collides with an `Object.prototype` member. (2) WHICH `number` PARAMETERS THE SOURCE TYPES `int`: exactly one, `cooldown_sec`, guarded with `Number.isInteger(x) && x >= 0` and pinned by a target-only case. There is no other number in the module: the two timestamps are ISO-8601 strings on both sides.

THE `datetime` TRANSCRIPTIONS LIVE IN `src/attention/pytime.ts`, NOT PRIVATELY IN THIS MODULE, and that is a decision rather than a layout preference. `dedup.py` and `classifier.py` both round-trip an ISO-8601 timestamp through `datetime` and both depend on CPython's exact answers -- `fromisoformat`'s grammar, which is narrower than `Date.parse`'s and reads a naive value as UTC rather than as local time, and `isoformat`'s rendering rule, which prints no fractional part at zero microseconds and six digits otherwise. A1 wrote both privately inside `src/attention/classifier.ts`; two private copies of one CPython function inside one directory is the drift shape rule 11 names, where the copies agree on the day they are written and nothing goes red on the day they stop. `D-0904` records the arrangement and what A2 did about A1's copies.

ONE INHERITED LIMITATION, CARRIED RATHER THAN REPAIRED, and it is A1's disclosure rather than a new one: a `Date` resolves to one millisecond and a `datetime` to one microsecond, so a parsed microsecond field is rounded into the millisecond and a stored timestamp within a fraction of a millisecond of a cooldown boundary can be judged on the other side of it from the source. Repairing it means carrying an epoch in microseconds through every consumer of `parseIso` instead of a `Date`, which is a change to the attention belt's shared vocabulary rather than to one module, and it belongs in the change that makes it -- not in the sub-belt that happens to be the second one to need the function. A sub-second UTC offset (`+23:59:59.999999`, which CPython parses) rounds into the same millisecond and is handled rather than dropped: an earlier draft stripped the fraction and put the instant a whole SECOND away, which the differential check against CPython caught. The WRITE side has no such limitation: `pyIsoUtc` renders the full six digits the source renders, so a timestamp this port writes and re-reads round-trips exactly.

WHAT `pyJsonDumps` BUYS OVER `JSON.stringify`, since the substitution is visible in the diff and is not merely stylistic. `json.dump(..., sort_keys=True)` sorts by CODE POINT and `JSON.stringify` over an object emits integer-like keys FIRST regardless of insertion order, so a dedup key that looks like an integer -- and `event:<id>` does not, but `pending:<task_id>:<kind>` is composed from an operator-supplied task id -- would land in a different position in the file on the two sides. The module reuses the port's existing CPython `json.dumps` transcription rather than growing a second local rendering of the same function, which is the same rule-11 argument the note above makes about `datetime`.

THE JSON PARSE IS `JSON.parse`, NOT `pyJsonLoads`, and the one place the two runtimes disagree lands on the same answer. `json.loads` accepts the bare literals `NaN`, `Infinity` and `-Infinity`, which `JSON.parse` rejects. Under the fail-closed repair both readings refuse the document -- this one at the parse, the source's Python counterpart one step later when the non-string value reaches the namespace reader -- so the divergence is not observable through this module's surface. `pyJsonLoads` was not used because its work is recovering the source text's key order and number spellings for re-emission, and this module re-emits through `pyJsonDumps` with `sortKeys: true`, which discards both by construction.

THE UNDECODABLE-BYTE PATH, WHICH THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS LEDGER GOT WRONG. `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on an undecodable byte; that is a `ValueError`, so it escapes the source's own `except OSError` and takes the watcher down. The first draft of this module read the file with `readFileSync(path, "utf8")` and this note said the outcome was a refusal either way, at the JSON parse. That was false for the case that matters: a bad byte INSIDE a JSON string leaves the document syntactically valid, Node substitutes U+FFFD, the parse succeeds, and the state loads with a key that is not the key that was written. The module now reads bytes and decodes with a fatal `TextDecoder`, so an undecodable file is refused rather than silently altered -- which is D-0904's fail-closed answer, not the source's crash. Found by the codex review gate, pinned by a target-only case, probe R1.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a missing file loads as empty state
entries.reason: Straight translation. `tmp_path / "missing.json"` is `join(caseRoot("dedup"), "missing.json")` and `state == DedupState()` is `toEqual(new DedupState())`. This is the ONE recovery path the fail-closed repair leaves standing, and it is left standing deliberately: an absent file is not malformed state, it is the absence of state, and creating one is the legitimate next step. `D-0904` draws that line explicitly so the repair cannot be read as "refuse everything".

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > state round-trips through save and load
entries.reason: Straight translation. The two assertions are spread over the namespaces exactly as the source spreads them. `loaded.events == state.events` becomes `toEqual` over spread copies rather than over the maps themselves, because both are built with `Object.create(null)` (rule 9, see the module note below) and spreading them into ordinary objects is what makes the failure output readable; the compared CONTENT is unchanged.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > malformed JSON is refused, not read as empty state
entries.reason: **Asserts the opposite of its source, by ratification.** The source writes `{ this is not json`, requires `load_state` to return `DedupState()`, and requires the word `recovering` on stderr. `PORTING_LEDGER.md`'s row for `attention/dedup.py` rules that behaviour out for durable dedup state -- an empty ledger says nothing has been notified, so every already-handled event is free to fire again -- and `D-0034` ratified the fail-closed repair as A2's, with `D-0023` requiring the case that pinned the inherited behaviour to be inverted in the same change. The same input is written; the assertion is `DedupStateRefused` with a message naming the file and saying it is not valid JSON. The `capsys` half has no counterpart because there is no longer a warning to capture: the refusal IS the report, and it reaches the caller rather than only the terminal. Recorded `adapted` rather than `waived` because the target case is stronger than its source in the property both are about -- the source lets a corrupt file through silently, this one cannot -- and `D-0034` names `adapted` as the notation for this belt's mechanism changes. Probe P1: replacing the refusal with `return new DedupState()` turns this case red with `expected DedupStateRefused to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a top-level that is not an object is refused, not read as empty state
entries.reason: The second of the two cases `parity/source-inventory.belts.md` and `PORTING_LEDGER.md` name explicitly, inverted for the reason the entry above gives. The source writes `[1, 2, 3]`, requires empty state and requires `recovering` on stderr; the target writes the same document and requires `DedupStateRefused` naming the file and the top level. `Array.isArray` is checked alongside `typeof === "object"` because a JSON array is an object in this runtime and is not a `dict` in Python -- without it the array would reach the namespace reader and be accepted as a document with no `events` key, which is the same silent-empty outcome under a different name. Probe P2: replacing the refusal with `return new DedupState()` turns this case red with `expected DedupStateRefused to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a document carrying only one namespace loads with the other empty
entries.reason: Straight translation, and the case that fixes where `D-0904`'s boundary falls. A document with `events` and no `pending` loads with `pending` empty, exactly as the source's `data.get("pending")` gives. This is NOT the repaired defect: an absent key is an absent namespace, the same class of fact as an absent file, and it is the one of the source's four recovery paths that survives untouched. The neighbouring shapes the source ALSO empties silently -- a `pending` that is present and is not an object, an entry that is not a string -- are refused, and each is pinned by its own target-only case below, so the line between the two readings is asserted rather than merely described.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > an event recorded once is never notified again
entries.reason: Straight translation, including the year the source jumps forward: `now=_NOW + timedelta(days=365)` is `plusSeconds(365 * 24 * 60 * 60)`. The point of the year is that the `state.db.events` namespace has no cooldown at all, and the keyword arguments become one options object under this port's own call convention, which changes no value.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a pending key inside its cooldown window is blocked
entries.reason: Straight translation: record at `_NOW`, ask again 200s into a 300s cooldown, require `false`.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a pending key past its cooldown window notifies again
entries.reason: Straight translation: the same setup 400s into a 300s cooldown, requiring `true`. Together with the case above it pins both sides of the boundary, which is why neither is enough on its own.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > a garbled stored timestamp counts as never notified
entries.reason: Straight translation of the assertion, and the case that made this port's `fromisoformat` transcription necessary rather than optional. The literal `"garbled"` is refused by `Date.parse` too, so this case alone would stay green over `new Date(text)` -- and `Date.parse` accepts shapes `fromisoformat` rejects (`"05/12/2026 11:59:00"`) and reads a naive value as LOCAL time, both of which turn a garbled stored value into a RECENT one and block the notification this case exists to let through. Two target-only cases below carry those inputs; this entry is the ported half and its assertion is unchanged.

entries.target_id: test/attention/dedup.test.ts::attention dedup > save replaces an existing file and leaves no temporary behind
entries.reason: Straight translation. `mkstemp(prefix=".attention_notified.", dir=parent)` plus `os.replace` becomes an exclusive-create (`flag: "wx"`, mode `0o600`) of a `.attention_notified.<random>` file in the destination directory followed by `renameSync`; `json.dump(..., indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True)` plus the trailing newline becomes `pyJsonDumps(..., { indent: 2, ensureAscii: false, sortKeys: true })` plus the same newline, which is the port's existing CPython `json.dumps` transcription rather than a second local rendering. Both of the source's assertions are kept, the parsed document and the empty leftovers listing. The FAILURE half of the same discipline -- that the temporary is removed when the write fails -- is not asserted by the source and is a target-only case below.
